summary: This document presents a security threat analysis for RPL, the routing protocol for low-power and lossy networks. It uses a systematic approach to define and assess the threats; countermeasures depend on the application.

eli5.summary: Tiny sensor networks pass messages along routes, and attackers might mess with them. This RFC lists the possible attacks.

questions: what are the security threats to rpl
what is a sybil attack in routing
how does rpl handle replay attacks
subtitle: A catalogue of the ways attackers can break routing in tiny, battery-powered mesh networks, and what can be done about each.

tldr.problem: RPL builds routes for low-power and lossy networks (LLNs) made of small, cheap, often unattended devices. Those constraints make routing easy to attack and hard to defend.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC models a generic routing process, applies the ISO 7498-2 security model (plus availability), then lists threats under authentication, confidentiality, integrity and availability, with countermeasures for each.
tldr.outcome: It is a threat analysis, not a protocol. The actual countermeasures are left to application-specific applicability statements, and some threats, such as key provisioning, are not solved by RPL itself.

today: RFC 7416 is an Informational document published in January 2015. The unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It is a companion to the RPL specification in RFC 6550.

sections.title: Why Routing Security Is Hard in LLNs
sections.content:
Many networked devices ship with minimal resources: little RAM, slow clocks, small storage, tight duty cycles and small packets. Some have no user interface at all, or are built to be safe near things like gas meters. The resulting Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) lose traffic easily and are more prone to vulnerabilities.

This RFC analyses threats to RPL, the routing protocol for LLNs defined in RFC 6550. It scopes itself to control-plane traffic, so it does not cover authorization or authentication of application traffic. Because there are many ways to solve each problem and the trade-offs depend on the deployment, the specific countermeasures are detailed in applicability statements, not here.
sections.eli5: Tiny gadgets have very little memory and power, so they are easy to trick. This note lists the tricks so people can plan defences.

sections.title: Assets, Access Points and the Security Model
sections.content:
The analysis starts from a data flow diagram of a generic routing process: nodes discover neighbours, exchange route and topology information, generate routes and use them to forward. From this the RFC lists assets (routing and topology information, the route generation process, channel bandwidth, node resources such as computing capacity, memory and energy, and node identifiers) and points of access (neighbor discovery, route/topology exchange, and the node's physical interfaces).

It then applies the ISO 7498-2 model: authentication, access control, confidentiality, integrity and non-repudiation. Non-repudiation is dismissed for routing, since logging and per-exchange signature checks would be an unsupportable burden on LLN devices. The RFC adds availability as a further requirement, meaning that routing exchanges and forwarding must work when needed.

Threat sources are the two classes described in RFC 4593: outsiders and Byzantine (insider) attackers.
sections.eli5: First you list what is worth protecting, like the map and the batteries, and every door a thief could use. Then you ask what could go wrong at each door.

sections.title: What Makes LLNs Special
sections.content:
The RFC draws on the urban, industrial, home and building automation requirements documents to list issues that are specific to or amplified in LLNs:

  • Limited resources: a security scheme that is light on memory can be costly in energy if keeping security state in sync is expensive, and syncing with sleepy nodes is complex.
  • Large scale and long life: an urban deployment can have several hundreds of thousands of nodes, and network lifetime is measured in decades, which complicates key management.
  • Autonomous operation: networks self-form and self-organise, so manual configuration is not an option.
  • Highly directional traffic: much traffic flows to and from LLN Border Routers, so advertising false preferred routes can do serious damage. Any node might end up in a sensitive position, so all nodes should be capable of being fully secured.
  • Unattended locations, mobility, and multicast and anycast support.

The resulting objectives include protecting routing information integrity in transfer and storage, ensuring only authorized entities use it, keeping it available, and ensuring authorized peers authenticate during neighbor discovery. Authentication must be bootstrapped and credentials need a flexible expiration scheme.
sections.eli5: These networks are huge, run for decades, sit in places nobody watches and have no one to set them up by hand. That makes keeping secrets and checking identities much trickier than at home.

sections.title: Threats and Attacks
sections.content:
Threats are grouped by the security service they undermine.

Authentication failures: if an attacker can join with any identity it can impersonate a node, act as a dummy node, or keep joining with new random identities to drain battery, RAM and bandwidth (node resource spam). Impersonation also lets it direct traffic to itself.

Confidentiality: exposed routing exchanges and topology reveal which nodes are important targets. Physical device compromise and remote device access are called device-specific issues that are out of scope for RPL to defend against.

Integrity: falsified routes (overclaiming and misclaiming), routing information replay, Byzantine attacks and identity attacks such as Sybil attacks can cause suboptimal or partitioned networks, premature node failure and black holes.

Availability: routing exchange interference (replay, ACK spoofing, overload), forwarding disruption (selective forwarding, wormhole and sinkhole attacks), and node resource exhaustion (Sybil, replay, HELLO-type floods, overload). Attacks on the underlying transport, such as RF jamming, cannot be countered by the routing protocol and are out of scope.
sections.eli5: A bad guy can pretend to be someone else, listen in, change the notes, or simply flood everyone so the batteries run out.

sections.title: Countermeasures
sections.content:
For each attack the RFC discusses what helps, and is frank about gaps.

  • Eavesdropping: encrypt all routing exchanges, with the mandatory-to-implement AES-128 in CCM mode (RFC 3610). The hard part is provisioning keys, which RFC 6550 does not solve. Traffic analysis can only be fully countered by tunneling with encryption over the original addresses.
  • Replay: an older message with a lower DODAGVersionNumber is rejected as stale, and a literal replay of a current message is generally harmless to the topology.
  • Overclaiming and misclaiming: RPL has no specific mechanism, so implementations may use local heuristics.
  • Byzantine attacks: RPL is a distance vector protocol, so nodes cannot directly detect them. It has no S-RIP-style mechanism, but it listens to multiple parents and may switch parents if it suspects it is being lied to.
  • HELLO flood and ACK spoofing: the DAO and DAO-ACK exchange checks bidirectionality, and L2 or L3 authentication defends well.
  • Overload: traffic quotas, isolating nodes above a threshold, and forwarding only trusted data.
  • Selective forwarding and sinkholes: multipath routing over disjoint paths, dynamically choosing the next hop, and geographic information for flow control.
  • Wormholes: a pure wormhole is nearly impossible to detect, and RPL uses hysteresis in its objective functions to cope with unstable links.
sections.eli5: Some tricks have a fix, like locking messages in code or checking dates on notes. Others, like a sneaky pair of friends passing notes through a secret tunnel, are very hard to spot.

sections.title: RPL Security Features and Key Management
sections.content:
The RFC sums up what RPL deployments should do. Because RPL uses multicast, those messages MUST be secured with the same services, and nodes MUST provide physical tamper resistance suited to the application environment.

Confidentiality is not essential to routing itself but reduces the effect of other attacks: use L3 payload encryption from RFC 6550 or L2 confidentiality. Integrity requires running RPL with only the secure message versions or over an L2 that binds node identity to transmissions. A single network-wide L2 key cannot give much integrity, because any holder can impersonate any node. Per-link keys do better for unicast but not for broadcast DIO messages, so RPL offers asymmetric authentication at L3 for the DIO. Availability measures nodes MAY use include limiting neighborhood size, using multiple paths and destinations, setting quotas and using geographic information.

An LLN MUST have a process for initial key and credential configuration and secure storage, and is encouraged to automate revocation and replacement. Some secure modes are impractical without public key cryptography, which many consider too expensive.
sections.eli5: The rule of thumb is to lock the doors, check who is knocking, and keep spare routes in case one gets blocked. The hardest part is handing out the keys safely.
